transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2028-11-06
Start: 16:00 PT
Duration: 62 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Luis Ortega (Redwood SE), Elena Park (Arcadia CTO), Tom Briggs (Arcadia Staff SRE), Priya Nair (Arcadia Sr ML Engineer)

Summary:
This was a technical deep dive focused on repeated p99 spikes observed by Arcadia on their on-prem inference cluster when using streaming responses. The discussion covered KV cache hotkeys and shard imbalance, streaming vs non-streaming tradeoffs for tail latency, batching/windowing strategies, quantization impact on memory bandwidth and CPUs, and VPC/on-prem networking (SR-IOV, jumbo frames, egress hops). The call ended with concrete next steps: run a targeted benchmark (3 prompt sets), try KV shadowing and adaptive batching, and schedule an on-prem connectivity test.

Topics: [p99, p95, streaming, batching, kv cache, quantization, VPC, on-prem, coldstart]

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — we'll give about an hour, do a quick context recap and then dive into the p99 spikes and potential mitigations. Luis is our SE and will drive the technical bits. Elena, Tom, Priya, you good with that order?
[00:12] Elena Park: Yep that's perfect. We've been seeing intermittent p99 increases that line up with traffic bursts. It's mostly on our on-prem cluster behind the edge load balancer.
[00:22] Luis Ortega: Cool, can you describe the topology quickly? where's the KV cache in your stack, and are you streaming tokens to the client or using discrete responses?
[00:33] Tom Briggs: Sure. Topology is two racks, each with 8 nodes - GPU inference boxes. We have an NGINX edge, then a local VPC-style network, then the Redwood runtime as a container set. KV cache is local to each node, sharded by token prefix using a simple mod hash, and yes we're streaming to clients for lower perceived latency.
[00:50] Priya Nair: We think hotkeying happens with a few popular prompts, and when the cache misses we see the p99 shoot up. p95 typically stays fine around 80–120ms but p99 jumps to 700–1.2s during those bursts.
[01:10] Luis Ortega: That pattern suggests uneven KV distribution + cold cache churn plus the streaming backpressure. Streaming reduces first-token latency but can amplify tail when the backend stalls on a miss or a KV rehydrate. A few quick axes: 1) KV sharding/replication, 2) prefix caching and shadowing, 3) adaptive batching windows, 4) quantization/compute bottlenecks, 5) network egress/serialization.
[01:35] Maya Chen: Quick qualifier — Arcadia is on our Private offering, correct? with customer-managed on-prem runtime? I want to check which features you've enabled, like pre-warm and prefix cache.
[01:45] Elena Park: We're on Redwood Private, yes. Pre-warm is on for a subset but prefix cache isn't enabled globally because of memory constraints.
[01:54] Luis Ortega: Ok, good to know. So for KV hotkeys, first suggestion is shadowing — we route a small percentage of requests through a shadow KV layer that records misses and warms remote replicas without impacting the live path. That reduces cold rehydrate events.
[02:12] Tom Briggs: How intrusive is shadowing? Does it add a hop or extra I/O latency while it's warming?
[02:18] Luis Ortega: Shadowing is async — it shouldn't add to the critical path. We write to a warm queue and a background worker populates local shards. There is overhead in memory and additional traffic between nodes, so packing that in your rack with high-throughput NICs helps.
[02:33] Priya Nair: On the sharding, we currently use mod-hash on prefixes. Would consistent hashing help? We can re-shard but worried about balancing and local hot replication.
[02:43] Luis Ortega: Consistent hashing with virtual nodes helps rebalance without big reshuffles. Also consider LRU eviction tuned to keep top-n prefixes pinned (pinning policy) and a small replica set for the hot keys — 2 replicas across racks can absorb spikes faster.
[03:00] Elena Park: We observed that spikes correlate with client-side bursts where they open many streaming connections simultaneously. Could the streaming multiplexing be the problem?
[03:10] Maya Chen: Streaming connection density can contribute — each streaming connection holds a netpoll/epoll resource and can backpressure. We usually recommend multiplexing multiple logical requests over fewer physical TCP connections where possible, or limiting concurrent streaming sessions per client.
[03:26] Tom Briggs: Any advice on batching windows? We already have continuous batching, but we see that increasing max delay reduces first-byte latency which we don't want.
[03:36] Luis Ortega: It's a trade-off. For p95/p99 you want adaptive batching: short windows for latency-sensitive but burst-aware expansion when backlog increases. We implement dynamic window growth: base window = 8ms, expand up to 40–60ms under load, and we also do cost-aware batching where heavy-token prompts get smaller batch caps.
[03:56] Priya Nair: That dynamic window sounds promising. Does the runtime support token-aware batching so long sequences don't monopolize the batch?
[04:05] Luis Ortega: Yes, we do token-aware priorities — estimates per-request token horizon and do head-of-line scheduling. Also continuous KV cache prefetch: if we see a pattern that a prefix is likely next, we prefetch the KV shards asynchronously.
[04:20] Elena Park: Quantization question — we were testing q4 and int8. Could quantization increase jitter due to CPU/GPU memory bandwidth differences?
[04:29] Luis Ortega: It can. Lower precision reduces compute but can change kernel selection and memory footprint. On some GPUs int8 kernels use different memory paths; if your PCIe or NUMA domains are suboptimal you can see jitter. Also consider kernel warmup — first few runs pick different kernels until warmed. We usually recommend steady-state warmup before measuring p99.
[04:49] Maya Chen: Follow-up — are you using SR-IOV or passthrough on the NICs? That matters for per-connection latency and multi-tenant noise.
[04:57] Tom Briggs: We're using standard bridge mode, no SR-IOV yet. We can enable SR-IOV but it's a change.
[05:03] Luis Ortega: Bridge mode can add CPU overhead. SR-IOV reduces host CPU jitter by letting each VF bypass some layers. Also enable jumbo frames in your rack if link supports it — reduces per-packet CPU interrupts.
[05:15] Priya Nair: We also noticed p99 spikes when one rack started doing heavy quantized model export jobs — could IO saturation on the host be causing cross-container tailing?
[05:25] Luis Ortega: Absolutely. Ensure isolation (cgroups, isolcpus) and test with network and disk IO noise. We can also suggest moving model compile/export to off-peak windows or to separate nodes.
[05:36] Elena Park: Are there any Redwood-side runtime knobs we should flip immediately to test impact?
[05:42] Luis Ortega: A few low-risk experiments: 1) enable prefix pinning for top-100 hot prefixes, 2) set KV replica factor to 2 for hotkeys, 3) switch streaming to chunked non-streaming for a small client cohort to observe tail change, 4) enable dynamic batching with a conservative max window (40ms). Any of these can be toggled per-route.
[06:00] Tom Briggs: For the chunked non-streaming test, what effect do you expect on p95 vs p99?
[06:08] Luis Ortega: Non-streaming typically increases median but reduces tail variance because the entire generation is scheduled as one unit and you avoid connection-level backpressure. Expect p95 to rise maybe 10–30ms but p99 could drop significantly if the tail was caused by streaming stalls.
[06:24] Maya Chen: Let's talk measurement: how do you recommend we capture the events? We need to align logs across edge, runtime and node-level.
[06:33] Luis Ortega: Correlate traces with a unique request_id, sample full token timings for slow requests, export KV miss counters, CPU/mem per-container metrics, NIC queue depths. We provide a diagnostic bundle script that collects dmesg, iostat, nvtop, and metrics — I'll include that.
[06:50] Priya Nair: Any comment on fallback models? We've been thinking of falling back to a smaller quantized variant on high-latency paths.
[06:59] Luis Ortega: Fallbacks are effective. We recommend a policy: if tail latency surpasses SLO for X% of requests in a sliding window, route new requests to a cheaper/quantized model with a fast-path optimized kernel. Combine with throttling or queuing storefront.
[07:13] Elena Park: Is there risk of quality regression with aggressive quantization or fallback?
[07:18] Maya Chen: Yes, so pair fallbacks with per-prompt eval sets and quality monitoring. Redwood Optimize can run lightweight evals and flag regressions; we can set automated rollback if quality drops beyond threshold.
[07:29] Tom Briggs: Back to networking — you mentioned multi-hop egress. Our VPC overlay occasionally nat's across a firewall to reach an external logging service. Could that extra hop explain some p99 spikes?
[07:40] Luis Ortega: Extra hops, synchronous logging or blocking callbacks are common culprits. Make logging async, and avoid blocking outbound calls in the request path. If external services are necessary, add local buffering or circuit breakers.
[07:53] Priya Nair: For the KV hotkey mitigation, any simple heuristics besides pinning? We've thought of time-decaying counters to detect emerging hotkeys.
[08:02] Luis Ortega: Time-decayed counters are good. Combine with bloom filters to detect likely hits and prefetch. Also consider tiered cache: L1 in-memory local, L2 remote within rack (faster), L3 remote across racks.
[08:15] Elena Park: Ok, that makes sense. Can you outline what you'd need to run the bench and try shadowing?
[08:22] Luis Ortega: We'll need: representative prompt sets (3 categories: short, medium, long), client concurrency profile (RPS and bursts), sample payload sizes, and access to a diagnostic endpoint or a short-lived agent to collect node metrics. Also network topology and whether SR-IOV can be toggled.
[08:40] Tom Briggs: We can provide the prompts and a week-long traffic dump. SR-IOV will take change control but we can plan it in the test window.
[08:48] Maya Chen: Great. We'll prepare a bench plan: baseline run (current config), shadowing run, and chunked non-streaming cohort. We'll include expected metrics to collect and dashboards.
[08:59] Elena Park: Any security/compliance concerns for on-prem testing? We need to check with infra — we use KMS for keys and keep logs in-house.
[09:07] Maya Chen: No external data egress by default. We'll share our SOC2 packet and private deployment docs. For benching we can run entirely within your network and only exchange small diagnostic bundles.
[09:20] Priya Nair: One more question on batching and tail — we saw some token explosion in certain prompts where the model emits long tokens due to hallucination, that throws off batching heuristics. Any advice?
[09:30] Luis Ortega: You can set per-route max-token caps and implement early-stopping heuristics. Also token-aware priority scheduling will limit long-run sequences from blocking short ones.
[09:40] Maya Chen: ok wrapping up, we'll send the runbook, propose the config diffs, and schedule the connectivity test. Anything else from Arcadia?
[09:48] Elena Park: No, that covers it. Thanks everyone.
[09:51] Tom Briggs: Thanks. We'll collect the prompt sets and send before Thursday.
[09:54] Priya Nair: Thanks, talk soon.
[09:56] Maya Chen: Thanks all — end.
